At dusk, the city loosened its grip on the day. Buses sighed at the curb, windows turned gold, and somewhere above the traffic a single star practiced being visible. I sat on a bench with no destination, holding a paper cup of tea that was too hot to drink and too comforting to put down.

A bicycle chimed behind me, and its bright note hung in the air like an afterthought.

Across the street, a florist gathered buckets from the sidewalk. She worked without hurry, tucking loose stems into water, rescuing petals from the pavement. A man passing in a dark coat stopped to help her lift the largest bucket. They exchanged no words, only the brief, surprised smiles of strangers who have accidentally shared something good.

I thought about how much of life arrives this way: not as revelation, but as a small adjustment in the light. A door held open. A familiar song leaking through headphones. The smell of rain before anyone looks up. None of it asks to be remembered, and perhaps that is why it stays.

When my tea cooled, I drank it slowly. The star brightened. The florist carried her flowers inside, and the man continued wherever he had been going, his coat disappearing into the blue crowd.

For once, I did not reach for my phone or invent a lesson. I simply sat there, letting the evening be unfinished, letting myself be one more quiet thing the city had almost, but not quite, overlooked.
